title: CHAPTER XVII - OF OFFENCES AGAINST PROPERTY
overview: Study the complete IPC Chapter XVII sequence, Sections 378-462, alongside BNS Chapter XVII, Sections 303-334. The mapping is based on subject matter and statutory ingredients; a corresponding provision is not necessarily identical in wording, reach or punishment. These are explanatory study notes, not verbatim bare-act text.
objectives: Identify possession, dishonest intention, consent, movement, delivery, entrustment and deception in property-offence problems.
Match each IPC provision from 378 to 462 to the relevant BNS section, subsection or clause.
Distinguish theft, snatching, extortion, robbery and dacoity, including preparation and attempt offences.
Separate dishonest misappropriation, criminal breach of trust, receiving stolen property and cheating.
Apply the restructured mischief tiers and the separate forms of trespass, house-breaking and night aggravation.
Explain changed thresholds, expanded definitions, new provisions and the law applicable to the date of conduct.
transition: BNS Chapter XVII came into force on 1 July 2024 under S.O. 850(E), dated 23 February 2024. For earlier conduct, examine the IPC and the repeal-and-savings provision in BNS 358; the date a complaint is filed does not by itself select the substantive offence. Article 20(1) of the Constitution prohibits retrospective criminalisation and a greater penalty than the law allowed when the offence was committed. This crosswalk concerns central provisions; special and local laws require separate checking. The monetary thresholds in the user's IPC headings are historical, not current BNS thresholds.

groups.title: Of Theft
groups.explanation: Theft protects possession, not simply ownership. The prosecution must connect dishonest intention with movement of movable property out of another person's possession without consent. A good-faith claim to property may negate dishonesty, depending on the facts. BNS 304 introduces a named snatching offence: sudden, quick or forcible seizure of movable property from a person or their possession in order to steal. Do not call every snatching robbery; apply the additional ingredients of BNS 309. Section 305 is wider than the old dwelling-house provision. The community-service proviso in 303(2) requires all three conditions: value below Rs 5,000, first conviction, and return of the value or restoration of the property.

groups.title: Of Extortion
groups.explanation: Extortion involves delivery induced by fear; theft involves taking without consent. Threats may concern injury to body, mind, reputation or property, or injury to another person, within the applicable definitions. Completed extortion requires the induced delivery. BNS 308(3), (4) and (6) separately punish putting or attempting to put a person in specified fear in order to commit extortion. The subsection order changes: IPC 386 maps to 308(5), IPC 387 to 308(4), IPC 388 to 308(7), and IPC 389 to 308(6).

groups.title: Of Robbery and Dacoity
groups.explanation: Robbery is aggravated theft or extortion, not an independent alternative lacking those foundations. In theft-based robbery the specified violence or instant fear must be for committing the theft or carrying away the property. Extortion-based robbery additionally requires the offender's presence (sufficient nearness), instant fear and then-and-there delivery. Dacoity requires a statutory total of five or more conjoint offenders/present aiders. BNS specifically punishes preparation and assembly for dacoity. Joint liability under 309(6) and 310(3) has its own conditions; do not assume that the individual deadly-weapon aggravation in 311 automatically applies to every companion.

groups.title: Of Criminal Misappropriation of Property
groups.explanation: Property may be innocently received but later dishonestly converted. A finder taking reasonable steps to return property is different from someone who appropriates it while knowing, or having means to discover, the owner. Reasonable time and reasonable means are factual questions. Temporary dishonest conversion can suffice. The deceased-person offence requires knowledge of possession at death and that no legally entitled person has since possessed the property.

groups.title: Of Criminal Breach of Trust
groups.explanation: Start with entrustment of property or dominion over it, then identify dishonest use, conversion or disposal contrary to law or the relevant legal contract, or wilfully allowing another to do so. The special-capacity variants require entrustment in that capacity. Ordinary non-performance or an honest investment error is not automatically criminal. A servant stealing the employer's property is analysed under 306; a servant dishonestly diverting entrusted property is analysed under 316(4).

groups.title: Of Receiving Stolen Property
groups.explanation: The receiving offences depend on both the property's status and the accused's knowledge or reason to believe. BNS 317(1) expands the definition to include cheating-derived property. The special dacoity-source, habitual-dealing and concealment-assistance variants must be proved separately. The definition applies to relevant transfers/misappropriation/breach of trust within or outside India, but the property loses its stolen character when it reaches someone legally entitled to possess it.

groups.title: Of Cheating
groups.explanation: Sections 415-417 belong with Cheating, rather than Receiving Stolen Property. Identify the deception, inducement, dishonest/fraudulent intention or intentional harmful act/omission, and causal result required by the relevant limb. In a promise-to-perform case, dishonest intent at inducement distinguishes cheating from a later civil breach. BNS 318(4), the IPC 420 counterpart, is not a catch-all for every unpaid debt. Personation under 319 needs cheating through the specified false identity, including a real or imaginary person.

groups.title: Of Fraudulent Deeds and Dispositions of Property
groups.explanation: These offences target specified dishonest or fraudulent dealings, not every disputed transfer or financial failure. Section 320 concerns defeating lawful creditor distribution; 321 concerns preventing a debt/demand being available for creditors; 322 concerns a transfer/charge instrument containing the specified false particulars; and 323 covers concealment/removal or dishonest release of a claim. A title defect, a false statement and forgery are different issues: document-forgery offences in BNS Chapter XVIII require their own ingredients.

groups.title: Of Mischief
groups.explanation: Mischief requires intended or knowingly likely wrongful loss/damage through destruction or an injurious change in property or its situation. It may affect one's own or jointly owned property. BNS 324(3) provides up to one year for property damage, 324(4) up to two years for Rs 20,000 to below Rs 1 lakh, and 324(5) up to five years for Rs 1 lakh or more; each allows fine or both. Animal-value thresholds are removed in 325, and the old fire-damage thresholds are removed in 326(f). The specific water, transport, navigation, landmark and fire provisions must not be replaced mechanically by the generic value tiers.

groups.title: Of Criminal Trespass
groups.explanation: Criminal trespass concerns another's possession and the specified intent on entry or unlawful remaining. A civil title disagreement alone is not enough. House-trespass requires the specified premises; lurking requires concealment precautions. House-breaking includes six statutory entry/exit methods: a made passage, an unintended passage/scaling, an abnormally opened passage, opening a lock, force/assault/threat, or unfastening a known-fastened passage. BNS does not separately define the old night labels: after sunset and before sunrise appears in 331(2), (4), (6) and (8). Keep purpose-based house-trespass (332), preparation-based house-trespass (333), and closed-receptacle offences (334) distinct.

keyPoints: Theft: IPC 378-382 -> BNS 303, 305-307; snatching in BNS 304 is a distinct addition.
Extortion: IPC 383-389 -> BNS 308(1)-(7), with reordered aggravated subsections.
Robbery/dacoity: IPC 390-402 -> BNS 309-313; dacoity requires five or more.
Misappropriation: IPC 403-404 -> BNS 314-315; breach of trust: IPC 405-409 -> BNS 316.
Stolen property: IPC 410-414 -> BNS 317; cheating/personation: IPC 415-420 -> BNS 318-319.
Mischief: IPC 425-440 -> BNS 324-328; old value thresholds and some coverage change.
Trespass and receptacles: IPC 441-462 -> BNS 329-334; night definitions are integrated into aggravated provisions.
examFocus: For each problem state the date and applicable law; identify the property/possession, act, mental element, delivery or entrustment, and any violence, number of participants, special capacity, value or night condition. Cite the exact BNS subsection, apply each ingredient and explain any change from IPC. Do not conclude that a civil dispute alone proves fraud, breach of trust or trespass.

practice.question: A person pockets a phone, then a companion restrains the owner to enable escape with it. Is this necessarily only simple theft?
practice.answer: No. Consider theft-based robbery under 309(2): restraint used for carrying away the stolen property can supply the additional ingredient. Assess each participant's role and applicable joint-liability rule.

practice.question: An email threatens reputational injury unless money is sent, but no money or security is delivered. Which distinction matters?
practice.answer: Completed extortion under 308(1) requires induced delivery. The in-order-to-commit fear offence under 308(3) may apply if its ingredients are proved.

practice.question: Four people commit robbery. Does calling them a gang automatically establish dacoity?
practice.answer: No. Section 310(1) requires five or more conjoint offenders/present aiders. Identify any additional proven participant rather than assuming one.

practice.question: An employee takes cash from an employer's locked drawer; another employee diverts money entrusted for deposit. What is the key distinction?
practice.answer: The first may involve theft under 306; the second may involve breach of trust under 316(4). Entrustment and dishonest conversion must be established on the facts.

practice.question: A contractor honestly intends performance when taking an advance, but later fails to complete the work. Is that alone cheating?
practice.answer: No. A subsequent contractual breach alone does not prove dishonest inducement at the outset. Examine the statutory deception and intention requirements under 318.

practice.question: For a first conviction for theft of Rs 4,000 with full restoration, what special rule should be discussed?
practice.answer: The proviso to 303(2) prescribes community service when all its conditions are met. It does not legalise theft below Rs 5,000 or apply merely because the amount is small.

practice.question: Ordinary mischief causes loss of Rs 25,000. Is the historical IPC Rs 50 tier the BNS test?
practice.answer: No. Examine 324(4), covering Rs 20,000 and more but less than Rs 1 lakh, and check whether any more specific aggravated provision applies.

practice.question: A trespasser opens a locked door with a found key after sunset. Must a door be physically smashed for house-breaking?
practice.answer: No. Opening a lock can fall under 330(2)(d). House-trespass and relevant night conditions must also be established before applying 331.
